title: George Baquet in Philadelphia, 1940, and John Reed's bootleg labels
summary: Russell recalls seeing George Baquet at Wilson's Cafe in December 1940 and the spelling of his name, then John Reed and the pirated Jelly Roll Morton masters.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: We'd been talking about some of the, this is Bill Russell again, some of the musicians that I'd interviewed at various times preparing for the book Jazz Man, and other times after that, that we weren't able to talk to because most of them are dead now. We weren't able to interview them for our Jazz Archive directly here. One of them was George Bach K., whom I stopped to see in Philadelphia in 1940, fall of 1940. The actual date was December 15th, 1940, on the way when I was moving to Pittsburgh. And he was playing at a little restaurant, not a little one, quite a big one really, called Wilson's Cafe, about 51st and Walnut. And I noticed out in front of the place they had a sign with his name, George Bach K.'s orchestra, spelt B-A-K-A-Y. And he explained that nobody could pronounce the French or Creole spelling of it, so that he just wrote it out phonetically in English. Incidentally, Bung Johnson's widow claims to be a member of the Bach K. family, and she spells it quite different than that, too. Not on anything to do with English, but it's entirely different to French or Creole spelling, whatever it is. I won't go over these notes because they're rather sketchy, too. They're better than some of the notes I took. But they weren't taken right there. I wrote them probably when I got back on the train on the way to Pittsburgh. So I'll write those out a little bit more fully and send those in sometime. And Mrs. Rankin can remind me if I'm slow on it. But they won't be lost. I also have a couple of pages of information on George Bach K., which I obtained from John Reed about 1943. He had gotten all of this before 1941 when he lived in Philadelphia. He was connected with RCA Victor at that time. Incidentally, John Reed was a jelly fan, too, and obtained some of the unissued jelly masters from Victor files. It might be possible. Some of those were reissued, too. The bootleggers in New York, Sam Meltzer and Bolentino. I think one of the two issued some of those unissued masters that had never come out on Victor. I don't know if we can ever obtain those.
They were on some of the either Biltmore or British Rhythm Society. They used all sorts of phony names on those.
